section_title: Can a royal scepter stop the sharpened sword?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 8 Again the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 9 “Son of man, prophesy and tell them that this is what the Lord says: ‘A sword, a sword, sharpened and polished— 10 it is sharpened for the slaughter, polished to flash like lightning! Should we rejoice in the scepter of My son? The sword despises every such stick. 11 The sword is appointed to be polished, to be grasped in the hand. It is sharpened and polished, to be placed in the hand of the slayer. 12 Cry out and wail, O son of man, for the sword is wielded against My people; it is against all the princes of Israel! They are tossed to the sword with My people; therefore strike your thigh. 13 Surely testing will come! And what if even the scepter, which the sword despises, does not continue?’ declares the Lord GOD.

14 ‘So then, son of man, prophesy and strike your hands together. Let the sword strike two times, even three. It is a sword that slays, a sword of great slaughter closing in on every side! 15 So that their hearts may melt and many may stumble, I have appointed at all their gates a sword for slaughter. Yes, it is ready to flash like lightning; it is drawn for slaughter. 16 Slash to the right; set your blade to the left— wherever your blade is directed. 17 I too will strike My hands together, and I will satisfy My wrath.’ I, the LORD, have spoken.”

context_lines: The warning becomes a poem about a sword sharpened for slaughter and polished to flash like lightning. It is prepared for the hand of the one who will wield it.

The princes are threatened along with the people. Ezekiel is called to cry out, strike his thigh and clap his hands as the sword closes in. The repeated images press home the terror and certainty of the coming judgment.
In the BSB, the question about the scepter challenges confidence in royal power. The sword treats the scepter as a stick, and the testing may leave it no longer standing.
The Lord’s own declaration closes the poem. The judgment is presented as His announced act, rather than something a king’s title or the city’s former confidence can prevent.
common_interpretation_lines: [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/21.htm) emphasizes the seriousness with which the sentence is pronounced and announced. [Wesley](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/ezekiel/21.htm) connects the warning with the threatened end of Judah’s king and kingdom.

The wording about the rod or scepter is difficult, and older translations arrange it differently. The [Cambridge discussion of verses 10 and 13](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/ezekiel/21.htm) examines both a rod of chastisement and a royal scepter, favoring a connection with the royal house in verse 13. The BSB’s scepter wording places the emphasis on the failure of royal standing to secure the people against judgment.
god_plan_lines: [Hebrews 12:25–29](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/12.htm) warns against refusing the God who speaks and describes created things being shaken so that what cannot be shaken remains. Believers are receiving an unshakable kingdom and are called to thankful, reverent worship.

Hebrews is not explicitly quoting Ezekiel 21. It develops the larger contrast between what human confidence treats as secure and the kingdom God gives. The warning against refusal and the promise of that kingdom belong together.
